newsitem.title: FRANCE: France plays down fears over ECB independence.
newsitem.headline: France plays down fears over ECB independence.

text.p: France on Monday played down fears that politicians might undermine the independence of a future central bank (ECB) under its proposals for an economic council for countries in European monetary union.
Officials said a French call for an informal council to co-ordinate economic policies among EMU members in no way threatened the independence of the ECB.

France has come under fire, notably from the German Bundesbank, for its proposal that countries inside the euro zone meet informally to co-ordinate economic and exchange rate policies after the launch of the single currency in 1999.

"We have always said France wanted an informal stability council, respecting the principles of subsidiarity (devolving decisions to national level where possible), and fully respecting the independence of the central bank," a finance ministry official told Reuters.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis also said on Monday he did not have the impression there was any quarrel with the German government over the idea. "I did not get the feeling there were differences on this," he told a news conference.
The Bonn government made no comment on Monday on the proposed council, although officials in France and elsewhere have said previously it had support in Bonn.
"The French idea, in fact, was supported by Germany, by Belgium, by Luxembourg and by others," Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker told Reuters earlier this month.

Paris argues it is reasonable for countries which share the same currency to get together from time to time, either at the level of finance ministers or heads of state and government. The council would be similar to the Group of Seven rich nations forum. The G7 has no secretariat nor headquarters.

But coupled with French calls for a rise in the dollar, the demand for a euro-zone council has raised fears the new forum may be used to put pressure on the future European Central Bank to allow a soft euro to promote growth and cut unemployment.

Former Bundesbank head Karl-Otto Poehl warned on Saturday that any political pressure on the ECB would run counter to the Maastricht treaty, which guarantees its independence, and would have a "catastrophic" impact on financial markets.

"If financial markets became convinced that a European central bank could be forced by political pressure to conduct a deliberate policy of devaluing the euro against the dollar or the yen, there could be portfolio shifts of catastrophic proportions," he wrote in a newspaper article.
On Friday, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said any attempt to create a political power to influence monetary policy would be against the Maastricht treaty.

"Those with a suspicious turn of mind might wonder whether former Bundesbank president Karl-Otto Poehl has been recruited by his former colleagues to do a hatchet job on the French," David Coleman at CIBC Wood Gundy in London said.
French officials say the council would discuss fiscal policies and implement a budget stability pact agreed last December limiting budget deficits after the launch of the euro.

It would also discuss exchange rates, agreeing for example a common position on the euro in G7 talks, or co-ordinating links with European currencies outside the euro zone. The Maastricht treaty leaves governments responsible for exchange rates.
Economists said they saw little sign of a Franco-German rift that would undermine the euro's launch in 1999.
"That economic policies would need to be co-ordinated in a single monetary area is pretty elementary," Bernard Godement, senior economist at Daiwa Institute of Research Europe, said.

They noted that even in Germany, whose independent Bundesbank is being held up as a model for the European Central Bank, the government had overruled its central bank in the past on exchange rate matters.
This was the case when the government fixed the exchange rate between the east and west German mark at one-for-one in 1990, despite warnings this could be inflationary.
